fullText:
EL PASO, Texas (KTSM) — High school football is getting closer in the Borderland, and teams across the region are officially getting back to work.

In New Mexico, teams kick off their seasons Aug. 20, while Texas teams begin their seasons Aug. 27. KTSM's Nine Overtime will also return Aug. 28 with its first episode of the season.

As part of our high school football preview series, we begin with the Eastwood Troopers.

The UIL allowed teams to begin practices Monday, and Eastwood wasted no time getting on the field.

The Troopers held their first practice of the season at midnight, continuing a tradition that has become a staple of the program.

Eastwood is currently practicing on its baseball field while construction continues on the turf at Trooper Stadium. The team is expected to return to its home field Tuesday.

The Troopers are coming off a successful 2025 season, finishing with 10 wins, a District 1-6A championship and a playoff appearance.

Now, Eastwood will look to build on that success with plenty of experience returning on both sides of the ball.

Senior quarterback Kingston Jeffries returns to lead the offense, while junior running back Matthew Ramirez is also back in the backfield. On defense, defensive end Brandon Jury is one of the key returners for the Troopers.

With that experience back, Eastwood enters the 2026 season looking to make another push for a district championship and another playoff run.

"We're just hungry. I think one of the things when you come off success is it's really easy to be complacent, really easy to be satisfied. But I've never felt that from the kids all offseason. I think you'll see an even better team this year." Eastwood football head coach Julio Lopez said.

"We got the best offensive line. They are bigger and stronger. Our receiver group - we moved Bentley De Vries to wide receiver, and he's been good this offseason," Eastwood senior quarterback Kingston Jeffries said. "We have a lot of returning dudes like Jordan Nava. Honestly, every position we have is filled with a lot of skill."

The Troopers open the season Friday, Aug. 28, against Bel Air.

Eastwood's District 1-6A opener is scheduled for Sept. 25 against Eastlake.

title: Orioles’ Pete Alonso gets real about backing up talk after big game vs. Rangers
description: Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso had a big day against the Texas Rangers in a much needed win for his ballclub.
fullText:
Orioles' Pete Alonso gets real about backing up talk after big game vs. Rangers appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

The Baltimore Orioles needed a win over the Texas Rangers on Sunday in the worst way. Baltimore had lost five of their last seven games. If they wanted to stay in the race for the AL Wild Card, a victory on Sunday was essential. Thankfully, veteran slugger Pete Alonso came through.

Alonso strode to the plate five times against Texas, reaching safely in every plate appearance. He walked twice, swatted two home runs, and drove in four runs. Baltimore won 10-5, and that performance was a vital one for Alonso, as he explained after the game.

"You can't talk and be vocal if you're not doing it. For me, you've got to do it, and then you talk afterwards whenever there's time. But also, in order to be a leader, who have to have done it and continuously be doing it," the Orioles star said, via Andy Kostka of Diamondback Sports.

Alonso is not producing the elite numbers he did last season with the New York Mets. Still, his first season in Baltimore is going quite well for him on an individual level. The veteran slugger has 25 home runs, 75 RBI, and a .252/.346/.472 slash line in 118 games thus far.

The Orioles, as a whole, could be much better. Their win on Sunday improved their record to 57-61. Despite the unfortunate record, they remain just two games back of a Wild Card berth in the AL.

Baltimore certainly needed this win and will need to continue this momentum moving forward. The Orioles begin a three-game set against a Wild Card rival in the Minnesota Twins on Monday.

Teaching Coding When AI Can Write the Code
description: Now that AI can write code, a student's submission no longer shows what they really understand. Here, I share three approaches we're testing at the University of Texas at Austin.
fullText:
Now that AI can write code, a student's submission no longer shows what they really understand. Here, I share three approaches we're testing at the University of Texas at Austin.

For as long as we’ve taught programming, the student’s code has provided a window into the students’ thinking. Errors, the code structure, the awkward working solution—all of it showed how someone reasoned and where they got stuck.

It was never a clean window. Students have always copied, crammed, and borrowed, sometimes turning in work they didn’t fully understand. But the code still left clues. Generative AI has changed that: A finished program now tells us more about a student’s prompts than their ideas. And here’s the part that should unsettle us—often, the better the code looks, the less we can say about what the student actually learned.

This raises a bigger question: If AI can write code, should we still teach coding? I believe the answer is yes, at least for some students and situations. But that’s another topic. Here, I want to focus on the next step: If we continue teaching coding in a world with AI, how can we know if students are really learning?

Some schools have responded by trying to catch students. They use AI detectors, surveillance tools, locked-down browsers, stricter rules, and clearer honor codes. This has also led to more suspicion.

Some of these responses make sense. Teachers want to protect learning, and schools want to keep things fair. But using detection as the main way to assess students is weak. Stanford researchers found that popular AI detectors often falsely flagged writing by nonnative English speakers, with 61.22% of TOEFL essays in one study marked as AI-generated. OpenAI even retired its own AI Text Classifier in 2023 because it wasn’t accurate enough. If the company that created the tool can’t reliably detect AI, it’s probably not a good idea to base your honor code on it.

But detection isn’t the real issue. Even if we had a perfect detector, we’d still be asking the wrong question. Instead of asking, “How do we stop students from using AI?” we should ask, “How do we teach coding in a world with AI, making use of its benefits, while still being able to see if students are learning?”

We’re seeing this challenge with students at AET, the Arts and Entertainment Technologies Department at the University of Texas at Austin. Although my usual home is Computer Science, it so happens that AET is within the College of Fine Arts at UT, which offers many other ways to learn and assess: studio work, critique, rehearsal, revision, and performance.

In the arts, the final piece has never been the whole story. A painting doesn’t explain the choices behind it. A performance doesn’t reveal the rehearsals. A design board doesn’t show the discarded versions. A composition doesn’t tell you where the student struggled or what they finally learned to hear.

Art education has developed practices that focus on visible progress. Students bring in sketches and drafts, discuss influences, revisions, and failures, and rehearse, perform, and critique each other’s work while it’s still in progress.

At AET, we teach creative coding, which means programming to create art, design, games, or experiences. That doesn’t mean coding for poets. Our students—game designers, web developers, and programmers—start from scratch and learn advanced concepts in tools like Processing and p5.js. In the creative coding tradition, a program is often called a sketch, borrowing the term from the art world. It means something temporary, exploratory, and open to change—something you make, test, revise, and share.

So in creative coding, we were already leaning toward the studio model of sketches, experiments, iterations, and critique. Now we’re pushing that further as we rethink how we teach coding in an AI world. Here are three things we’re already using or actively developing.

We run the class like a studio. It’s not that work never happens at home, but the most important work needs to be seen in the classroom. Students show their code, including false starts, revisions, the choices they made, and the reasons behind them. Assignments are no longer just things you submit—they become projects you develop in public.

AI isn’t banned from the classroom. Instead, it’s treated as a helpful assistant to learn from. Students share prompts and techniques. They use AI, Google, Stack Overflow, classmates, or any other resources.

But you still need to take responsibility for your work. If you submit or present it, you must explain what the code does, why you made those choices, and how it works. If I need to ask your AI to understand your code, something is wrong. Getting help is fine, but hiding behind that help is not.

You can’t outsource to AI what the whole room watched you build.

A real studio needs students talking out loud together in the room every day. This also helps with another issue that isn’t about AI. Many people say students today are quieter than in the past. While this is mostly based on stories rather than long-term studies, these stories are common and consistent. Faculty on all types of campuses talk about silent classrooms and students who hesitate to speak up, especially since 2020.

Whatever the reason, this silence can be changed, and the solution is the same as for AI challenges: encourage students to participate. Communication is one of the most important skills in any career, including explaining ideas, defending choices, and persuading others in real time. Students don’t develop these skills by just submitting AI-guided work online. When they share their work publicly, it not only prevents AI misuse but also helps them build the skills they need most.

We know the usual pattern: A student asks, AI answers, and the student copies. We’ve tried to invert this. In our new approach, the AI works with the student on a set of topics, engages them in a conversation they must navigate, and ultimately assesses how well they understand the material, which leads to a grade.

This idea has a research background that goes back before ChatGPT. Teachable-agent systems like Betty’s Brain showed that explaining—even to a software agent—forces students to organize their knowledge, make connections clear, and find gaps. Our model uses this insight differently. The student isn’t teaching the bot. Instead, the student is having a conversation with it, learning, discussing, debating, and showing what they understand.

How did we do this? With fairly simple prompt engineering, we created an avatar chatbot of Vera Molnár (1924–2023), a pioneer of algorithmic art. The bot takes on Molnár’s role, drawing students into conversations about randomness, computation, generative art, and creative choices. Her practice sits exactly where creative coding students need to think: between rule and variation, system and choice, computation and visual judgment.

A system prompt sets the topics and types of questions to ask. The bot goes through these with the student, asks for more detail on unclear answers, and keeps following up until there is proof of understanding. At the end, it reviews the conversation against a rubric, giving us a clear record of which ideas the student covered, where they struggled, and how well they improved.

Besides the assessment, which is often accurate, the transcript becomes a different kind of proof, showing what a typical assignment might hide. What did the student notice? What did they misunderstand? Could they connect the concept to the code? Could they defend their choices? Could they revise their explanation when challenged?

When we switch the roles, something surprising appears: the one thing a finished submission can’t show.

Programming has never really had a tradition of performance. Musicians have it, painters have it, and dancers have it. Live coding is starting to change that.

Every semester at AET, students from different disciplines stage an algorave together—short for algorithmic rave. Audio sets, projection pieces, game demos, lasers, drones, experience design. The creative coding class brings live visuals into the live-coding tradition: Code is written and modified in real time, the screen is projected, and the audience watches the editor change as the visuals respond to the music other students are playing.

No prerender. No hiding the machinery.

The Live Coding manifesto, written in 2004 by TOPLAP, includes a line that fits every AI-era assessment conversation: “Obscurantism is dangerous. Show us your screens.” This is not just a performance ethic; it’s also an assessment strategy.

A student walks on stage. The projected screen is their editor. The room can read it. The music starts. And they build up a line of code on screen like:

osc(18, 0.08, 1.2)

 .modulate(noise(3), 0.25)

 .rotate(() => time * 0.1)

 .out()

This is JavaScript building visuals in real time. FFTs, chained functions, higher-order manipulations. When you’re manipulating code like that on stage, you’d better know what you’re doing.

AI can help you prepare. Good. Let it.

But once you’re on stage, the question shifts from “Can you copy and paste code?” to “Can you control it?” You can paste code into a file, but you can’t paste your way through three minutes of public debugging while the whole projection turns into a beige rectangle. In a live build, understanding has nowhere to hide.

Can you read the code, make changes on purpose, and recover when something unexpected happens? That’s fluency: knowing what to do next while the system is still running.

It is very hard to plagiarize panic.

So far, our results are based on our own observations. We haven’t conducted a controlled study or compared different groups, so what we have seen might just be early variation rather than patterns that apply more broadly. For now, these efforts are experiments, not final answers.

Assessment in studio and live performance settings is always subjective and focused on people. It relies on monitoring students’ progress, providing feedback, and observing how they handle challenges. We do not plan to change this core approach.

For the Molnár conversation assignment, students discussed Molnár using an AI system. The AI then created a summary and analysis of each student’s understanding. Teaching assistants reviewed this analysis, conducted their own assessments, and assigned grades. In our small experiments, the AI’s assessments using the rubric matched closely with the teaching assistants’ own evaluations.

We also used AI to help grade the end-of-term coding assignment. In this project, students improved an object-oriented game by adding strategies like heuristics, search algorithms, and learned behaviors. Since our teaching assistants had limited experience with object-oriented programming, we developed a detailed rubric and had an AI model use it to evaluate each submission. The AI’s analysis was given to the teaching assistants as support. It helped them see how each project was structured, spot important OOP design choices, and use the rubric with more confidence. The teaching assistants still made their own grading decisions. I was available as the OOP expert for any questions they could not answer. From what I observed, this substantially helped the teaching assistants understand and grade the students’ OOP design work.

More broadly, both approaches appear to enable substantive feedback at a scale that would otherwise be difficult given our current student-to-teaching-assistant ratios.

We spent the first two years of the generative AI panic asking how to catch students using AI—or prohibit it altogether. Wrong question.

The real question is whether the assignment gives students a real way to show and develop their understanding. This view isn’t limited to educators. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang recently argued that students should not focus on finding an “AI-proof” subject. Instead, he suggested they consider how AI can help them learn more deeply and develop their skills and sense of purpose. He highlighted storytelling, creativity, design, and judgment as abilities that will stay important even as AI takes over more tasks. This supports a key idea in coding education: The aim is not to prove you didn’t use any tools, but to help students show how they think, make choices, revise, and take responsibility for their work.

These three practices are experiments, not universal solutions. They work especially well in creative coding, where code already has a public, visual, and performative aspect. But they suggest a broader principle: As finished work becomes easier to generate, assessment needs to focus more on process, explanation, revision, and mastery.

This matters outside of school too. A polished memo no longer proves there was real thinking behind it. A working prototype no longer proves product sense. A passing pull request no longer proves the developer made the change carefully and thoughtfully. AI makes production easier, so evaluation must focus more on how people think, choose, revise, and recover—in code review, hiring, and performance management. The artifact is no longer the proof. The process is.

Generative AI didn’t make assessment impossible. It just made a hidden weakness obvious. We were putting too much trust in finished work. The arts always knew better.

title: Opinion - Are Republicans blind to the canaries in the Florida and Texas coal mines?
description: Maybe the warnings are not reaching certain ears in the administration and the Republican leadership.
fullText:
I have never understood how self-proclaimed or anointed election experts, who are wrong time and again, remain the go-to experts for much of the media. What I do understand is why they are wrong so often.

Many of these experts live in bubbles quite removed from Main Street America and especially the working-class voting population.

To be sure, Republicans have more than their fair share of the snobbish, pompous and the ignorant, living happily and hedonistically within those same bubbles of luxury that will never be attainable to many of their fellow Americans.

Having grown up in poverty myself, I can say that most in the working-class do not resent others' success.  They just want those who do attain or are handed that success to understand and address the plight of the disenfranchised and the powerless if they ever do find themselves in positions of power.

In my time, I have known many paycheck-to-paycheck parents and voters, many of whom still deeply believe in President Trump. And yet all say their paychecks buy less and less with each passing month.

My wife and I have done all right in life. But of late, every single time she comes back from the grocery chain store with just two small bags of items, she points out the ever-increasing prices.  This is no one's imagination. This is reality.

Some in the administration will claim until the cows come home that the stock market is doing great; 401(k) accounts are growing; and all of our rich friends are getting richer. But one truth for one class does not cancel out the quality-of-life crushing truth for another.

Politics, like much of life, is cyclical.  Democrats used to be really good at addressing bread and butter issues. Then Republicans cleverly hijacked that winning formula. And now, it seems to be swinging back toward the Democrats.

As we rapidly approach the midterms in November and the 2028 presidential election, history and reality are working against the Republicans. History reminds us that in 20 of the last 22 midterm elections, the party not occupying the Oval Office gained ground. That, coupled with the reality of more and more working class Americans struggling economically, should be a five-alarm warning for Republicans.

Yet, so many seem blissfully oblivious to it all.

As an example, I offer up the red states of Florida and Texas. Maybe the warnings are not reaching certain ears in the administration and the Republican leadership, but I well-connected Republicans in those two states are increasingly worried about the Senate race in Texas and the governor's race in Florida.

Aside from their concerns that the Republican Party is coming down on the wrong side of bread and butter issues, they worry that they are putting up flawed candidates in a midterm that already favors Democrats.

In Texas, a new Fox News poll shows Democratic senate candidate James Talarico (D) leading Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by 3 points. And among "extremely motivated voters" from both parties, Talarico's advantage in the race grows to 6 points. Even worse, one-quarter of non-MAGA Republicans support Talarico. All this in a state Trump won by 14 points in 2024.

Why? One reason is that Republicans are wasting time and money attacking Talarico's personal life. Another is Ken Paxton's personal flaws. A third is that working-class Texas feels shunned by Republicans promoting what is supposed to be a great economy based on 401(k) performances.

A similar situation exists in Florida. Every Republican I speak to in that state believes term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) to be "the best governor in the nation." Many also believed that his wife Casey would have been a lock to replace him, but we will never know. President Trump, as is his prerogative, endorsed Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) before the Republican primary for governor had even begun. The primary is still coming up, but Donalds will be the Republican nominee.

In the meantime, he is getting pounded by negative attack ads that will be used against him by the eventual Democratic nominee (most likely former Republican Congressman David Jolly, now a Democrat) this fall. Florida Republicans I know are nervous.

That, once again, comes on top of real economic pain felt by every paycheck-to-paycheck voter.  Karl Rove, who driving force behind George W. Bush election as president, has warned that "Republicans risk making the same political mistake he believes cost Democrats the 2024 election, arguing the party is relying too heavily on favorable gross domestic product and job figures while failing to address the economic pressures many voters still feel.

Even as Democratic Socialists of America gain ground with outright communists winning nominations, a multitude of "canary in the coal mine" examples exist on the Republican side as well, including in Florida and Texas. If both of these flawed canddates fail, the Republican Party is in deep trouble.

I am no expert, but if I were the Republican leadership, I might be trying to figure out how to get some emergency oxygen to these canaries before it is too late.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

title: Ryan Niblett names the three fastest Texas players, and the results will surprise you
description: A freshman tops the list.
fullText:
AUSTIN, Texas — Access to the Catapult GPS data tracked by the Texas Longhorns coaching staff isn't made accessible to the media or the public, so insight into the fastest players on the team has to come from sourced reporting, high school track times, companies like Reel Analytics that use AI to measure game film, and the players themselves.

On Thursday, following the second practice of preseason camp at Frank Denius Fields, redshirt junior running back/wide receiver Ryan Niblett, the team's dynamic return man, was asked about the three fastest players on the team. His response was surprising, and not just because he excluded himself, citing his humility.

"Kohen, of course," Niblett said. "Kohen's definitely fast."

That's freshman wide receiver Kohen Brown, a surprising pick thanks to his youth and relatively modest recruiting rankings — the Waxahachie product was the No. 266 player nationally and the No. 42 wide receiver in the 247Sports Composite rankings in the 2026 cycle.

With 41 offers, Brown was a coveted prospect when he committed to Texas last summer less than a month after receiving his offer from the Longhorns. And his 100-meter times from his junior season of high school are impressive with a 10.69 effort, but not the best on the team.

But Brown did impress head coach Steve Sarkisian with his physical development over the offseason and reportedly reached 23.1 miles per hour in summer conditioning, a number that Niblett may be referencing in placing Brown atop the team's speed chart.

Brown's speed flashed on a catch from freshman quarterback Dia Bell during the viewing period of Wednesday's practice.

Dia Bell to Kohen Brown. Dot. 🤘 pic.twitter.com/TWw5uZZPrq

Perhaps more impressive was how Brown tracked the ball over his shoulder.

The art of the catch from Texas freshman wide receiver Kohen Brown. Textbook tracking. Sees the ball into the hands. Stays inbounds in the corner of the end zone.

All of the good stuff. All in one reception. pic.twitter.com/TXgU65i9nr

As a true freshman, Brown doesn't project as a contributor on offense, but it may only be a matter of time as his trajectory shows signs of quickly outpacing his rankings.

The second player cited by Niblett was much less surprising — junior wide receiver Ryan Wingo, whose combination of size and speed made him a consensus five-star prospect through most of the 2024 cycle.

It's verified speed, too, as Wingo finished third in the Missouri 5A state championships in the 100 meters as a sophomore with a time of 10.55. After arriving on the Forty Acres, Wingo was one of the 10 fastest players in college football tracked by Reel Analytics last year, reaching 22 miles per hour, which slotted fifth overall, achieved on a post route touchdown catch against Sam Houston.

Fastest 5 College Football Players of Week 4

2️⃣ 22.0 mph – Texas WR Ryan Wingo (@_Ryanwingo1) #ReelSpeed 

🔗 https://t.co/qrL6HYSf3o pic.twitter.com/haDl6RMWga

Senior cornerback Warren Roberson was another surprising inclusion as the third player mentioned by Niblett — while the Red Oak product has surely improved his speed since arriving on the Forty Acres as a member of the 2023 recruiting class, his 100-meter times between 11 seconds and 11.27 seconds as a sophomore came five years ago, with his latest 200-meter time of 23.4 seconds as a junior.

Roberson's speed helps explain why he's been a core special teams player for coordinator Jeff Banks over the last two seasons, totaling 556 snaps on five units, but to build on his 187 snaps on defense last season, the 6'0 , 189-pounder will have to combine that speed with consistent technique and discipline.

There's a good chance he's in the top three after running a 10.58 100-meter dash and a 22.14 200-meter dash as a sophomore at Aldine Eisenhower six years ago.

With the Horns, Niblett hit 20.8 miles per hour on his punt return touchdown against Oklahoma in Week 7 last year, good for eighth nationally that week.

title: De Blasio: Talarico’s ‘kitchen table’ talk ‘worst nightmare for Republicans’
description: Former New York Mayor Bill de Blasio (D) said Tuesday that Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico’s discussion of “kitchen table issues” is Republicans’ “worst nightmare” as Democrats look t...
fullText:
Former New York Mayor Bill de Blasio (D) said Tuesday that Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico's discussion of "kitchen table issues" is Republicans' "worst nightmare" as Democrats look to clinch a Senate seat in the Lone Star State.

"When you listen to Talarico, he is going after billionaires. He's saying they're not paying their fair share of taxes. He is talking about commonsense kitchen table issues, which his opponent isn't," de Blasio told Fox News's Sean Hannity.

"This is the worst nightmare for Republicans that Democrats actually get their act together and talk about the kitchen table," he added.

Many 2026 midterm Democratic campaigns have focused on the idea of affordability for constituents, including Talarico's.

According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published this week, Democrats had a small lead over Republicans when it came to economic messaging for the first time in close to 10 years.

title: Texas judge rules that law regulating firearm suppressors and some guns can't be enforced
description: A federal judge in Texas on Wednesday struck down a 1930s law that imposed regulations on firearm suppressors and guns that are considered the most dangerous, more than a year after President Donald T...
fullText:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A federal judge in Texas on Wednesday struck down a 1930s law that imposed regulations on firearm suppressors and guns that are considered the most dangerous, more than a year after President Donald Trump signed a bill eliminating taxes on those items.

The ruling could allow firearm owners to purchase firearm suppressors — known as silencers — short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns and other certain firearms without registration, while also removing a layer of background checks. Last year, Republicans eliminated a $200 tax on those devices under Trump's massive tax and spending cut bill.

The regulations are required under the National Firearms Act, passed in the 1930s in response to concerns about mafia violence. Groups that support gun restrictions said the law still has important safety protections and criticized the ruling as reckless.

U.S. District Judge James Hendrix said because there were no longer taxes under the act, the regulation should not continue either.

"No longer can the challenged NFA provisions be justified — as they have been for nearly 90 years — under Congress's taxing power," Hendrix wrote.

The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, which enforces the regulations, did not immediately return an email seeking comment.

The National Firearms Act has been in effect since 1934 and establishes key differences and regulates firearms considered the most dangerous. Because the act implemented a tax on the item, the registration was often used to ensure the tax was paid, gun rights groups said.

The ruling was a major victory for gun rights groups who said they hoped the decision would create momentum to ultimately send the case to the U.S. Supreme Court.

"This ruling will set a precedent we can now argue in courts across the country to allow Americans to exercise their Second Amendment rights without fear of being placed on some government registry," the Second Amendment Foundation said in a statement.

While background checks will still be required under federal law, Giffords Law Center Chief Counsel Adam Skaggs said the registration process included notifying local law enforcement and asking if there was any reason to deny the application.

"That process effectively functioned as a heightened background check for NFA weapons, and that process is no longer enforceable," Skaggs said in a statement.

In June, the number of registered firearm suppressors in the U.S. was more than 6.4 million, according to the ATF.

"Today's ruling is a dangerous step backward for public safety," the Giffords Law Center, which advocates for tougher gun control measures, said in a statement.

Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Republicans want to talk about James Talarico’s manhood. Talarico says let them.
description: Democrats’ hopes to flip the Senate may hinge on the Texas candidate’s strategy to win back male voters.
fullText:
He's eating barbecue. He's winning over Joe Rogan. He's challenging his opponent to mano-a-mano televised faceoffs.

James Talarico is determined not to let his GOP challenger Ken Paxton's and Republicans' attacks on his masculinity define him in what has emerged as one of the party's loudest tactics in the crucial Senate race.

The Texas Democrat is working to position himself as a candidate focused on issues he says men actually care about instead of speculation about his diet, sexuality and religious beliefs.

"They've even called me a vegan, and those are fighting words in the state of Texas," Talarico said at a San Antonio rally this summer.

"Nowadays our culture tells young men that greatness is tearing other people down, is trolling and owning and dominating. But my dad showed me what real greatness looks like. He inspired me to serve," Talarico said at another rally in Houston, referencing how his dad often mowed the lawn of his elderly widowed neighbor without asking.

Talarico's attempt to reclaim the masculinity narrative by confronting the issue head-on could help propel him to flip a seat Democrats haven't held in nearly four decades, and which could determine control of the Senate next year.

It comes as both parties, in Texas and across the U.S., are fighting to win male voters — especially young, Black or Hispanic men — who in 2024 lurched to the right to help Republicans take control of the White House and Congress. The issue of masculinity has also been turbo-charged during Donald Trump's second term, with the president hosting UFC fights on the White House lawn and his Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth pushing for testosterone testing in the military.

If Talarico prevails, he could ultimately serve as a model for other Democratic candidates to connect with male voters or fend off Republicans who try to use issues of masculinity as a cudgel.

"Democrats need to be prepared for more of these attacks to come and understand how to handle them," Lucas Holtz, a senior political adviser at the centrist think tank Third Way, said in an interview.

Republicans think they've hit a nerve with Texas voters about Talarico's manhood. Members of the party have targeted the 37-year-old public school teacher-turned-state legislator for past statements endorsing a vegan lifestyle, suggesting that "God is nonbinary" and opposing legislation that erodes transgender rights.

"If you look at him, this is a guy who's publicly stated pretty bizarre things — that God is nonbinary," said Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) in an interview. "He's a total weirdo, and I think Texas voters recognize that."

Talaricosaid recently his comment on God's gender was meant to be "deliberately provocative" and that he meant God is beyond gender.

Republicans are also seizing on Talarico's unmarried status and smaller physical build to paint the Democratic candidate as weak and effeminate. Some have falsely called him gay or transgender. Paxton's very first ad of the general election campaign implied Talarico has low testosterone levels. And a conservative PAC released an AI-generated video of Talarico as an actress from "The Sound of Music" singing about wanting to give hormones to children.

Talarico opposes gender affirming care for minors, his spokesperson JT Ennis said.

"In Texas, there's a certain level of tough guy-ness that we all pretend to have in ourselves, and that we like in our elected officials," said Vinny Minchillo, a Texas-based Republican admaker who is not involved in the race. "If you push that the right direction, that especially does not sit well with Hispanic men and Black men."

Paxton's campaign and his allies think Talarico's previous comments on these issues put him out of touch with voters in both parties.

"Texans can spot an audition for a new identity and they know he is weak and woke on core Texas values," Paxton adviser Nick Maddux said in a statement. Maddux pointed to moves Talarico has made during the campaign he said shows flip-flopping, such as wearing a Texas flag shirt after calling the American flag a "complicated symbol."

"He is undoubtedly hurting Democrats," Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz said in an interview about Talarico.

Some Hill Democrats say Republicans' fixation on Talarico's manhood is an attempt to distract from Paxton's weaknesses.

"They fear his strength, especially since he's running against the most notorious scumbag in American politics," Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) said.

Paxton has faced an ethics complaint that was later dropped, a Justice Department corruption investigation for which he was not charged and securities fraud charges which were ultimately dismissed in an agreement. He was also impeached by the Texas GOP-led House for bribery and abusing his public office, which he called a "sham" coordinated by liberals, and was later acquitted by the Texas Senate.

Paxton also has a history of using cultural issues to his advantage, such as stoking anti-Muslim fears through campaign messaging.

Meanwhile, Talarico's campaign says they're not seeing evidence that the masculinity barbs are gaining traction, pointing to robust Democratic gains among Hispanic voters while also arguing that polling shows a toss-up general election contest. The campaign did not share specific data to support that its messaging to male voters was lifting Talarico's polling with that demographic.

Talarico has focused on issues he says affect many men — like lowering housing costs, stopping corporate landlord rent manipulation and curbing the influence of billionaire mega-donors in politics.

"Ken Paxton is picking these fights no one cares about to distract from the fact that he has no solutions to lower the cost of gas, groceries, or healthcare," Ennis said in a statement. "Real men serve others, weak men serve themselves."

Talarico also has tried to appeal to young men and Hispanic voters by placing ads during World Cup and NBA Finals games. And he's challenging Paxton to a series of televised debates, in which the two could spar on manhood and other issues. Paxton's team said he's agreed to the debates but they're still negotiating logistics and terms.

The Democrat's campaign also said it is trying to facilitate similar opportunities to Talarico's pivotal appearance on Joe Rogan's podcast last year, which boosted his national profile to millions of young men who make up Rogan's core audience. The podcaster — who during the interview exclaimed "you need to run for president," to Talarico — has continued to compliment the Texas Democrat and defend his views, including during a conversation with Vice President JD Vance last month.

Talarico has also fired back with his own jabs. He responded to Paxton calling him "Talafreako" by putting the phrase on T-shirts and selling them on his campaign website.

And Talarico turned on Paxton's low-testosterone message by telling MS NOW "I don't think guys my age are really concerned about that kind of thing," adding, "You've got these old guys lathered up in their fake tans throwing cheesy nicknames at each other."

Some public opinion research shows Talarico's strategy fits the 2026 moment.

The growing cost-of-living crisis — exacerbated by the deeply unpopular military conflict in Iran — and Trump's low approval ratings may mean the GOP's masculinity attacks fall flat this cycle, Luke Warford, founder and director of Texas Public Opinion Research, a nonpartisan public opinion research firm, said in an interview.

The top issues for men and young men in Texas center on affordability, the cost of living, economic growth and job creation, according to an aggregate of data shared with POLITICO from the group's latest surveys in May and June.

"We've got a really different scenario now where the Republicans are in power in Texas and nationally, so they own the things that are broken," Warford said. "There is a deep anti-establishment sentiment in this country and a deep frustration with the status quo particularly among men, and that could be a much stronger political force than the cultural attacks."

Matt Angle, founder of the Lone Star Project, a Democratic-aligned political action committee in Texas, said "there's no attack that should be ignored," but that Democrats are in a good position.

"Ken Paxton is no he-man. He's a thin-chested, soft spoken, weak guy," Angle said.

One warning sign for Talarico: a swath of male voters perceive him as too progressive, said Holtz, the Third Way adviser. Holtz noted a recent poll of men by the group in which 49 percent of respondents said the candidate was "too far left."

In focus groups held by the centrist think tank last year and this year, young men overwhelmingly pointed to the Republican Party as the better representative of men's priorities. Respondents in those groups associated Democrats with more social and cultural issues while tying Republicans with financial independence, finding a partner and starting a family.

On Capitol Hill, some Democrats are calling the conversation in Texas an opportunity to revisit the party's historic avoidance of issues that are important to men, which have made them more susceptible to criticism.

Rep. Marc Veasey, a moderate Texas Democrat, said in an interview that "Democrats, overall, need to do a better job of expressing some of the concerns that young men have."

"When we have people on our side who are attacking things like nuclear family structure and expecting everybody to fall in line, that's pure insanity," Veasey said. "There's this expectation with Democrats that men are just going to follow along, and they're not. We haven't figured out how to talk to them."

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said in an interview that Democrats tend to display examples of "traditional masculinity" rather than the "stereotypical masculinity" Republicans are attacking them for not adhering to. He pointed out he served in the Marines, Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) played football and Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) was an astronaut.

"What voters know is truly masculine is a politician who is going to take care of their needs and be a protector and be a provider for the family," Gallego added.

"When a man can't support his family because inflation is so fucking high, they're not going to care about who is on the ballot that is, quote unquote, 'not masc enough.'"

NEW YORK, Aug 2 (Reuters) - Kay Granger, a Texas Republican who was the first woman from her party ‌to chair the U.S. House of Representatives' powerful Appropriations ‌Committee, has died, her son J.D. Granger confirmed to Reuters on Sunday. ​She was 83.

No cause of death was given. Kay Granger in 2024 said she was battling "unforeseen health challenges."

Granger represented her Texas district in Congress from 1997 to 2025. In 2023, Granger announced ‌she would not seek ⁠re-election to the U.S. House of Representatives.

In her final term as a lawmaker, Granger chaired the ⁠House Appropriations Committee for more than a year, putting her in charge of spending legislation and making her one of the ​most influential ​members of Congress.

House Speaker Mike ​Johnson praised Granger as a ‌trailblazer. "Throughout her career, she broke barriers for women in public service," Johnson said, noting that she was the first female mayor of Fort Worth and the first Republican woman elected to represent Texas in the U.S. House.

She was the first Republican ‌woman to lead the budget panel, ​although two Democratic women, Representatives Nita ​Lowey and Rosa DeLauro, ​preceded Granger in the role.

"At every step of ‌her career, she [Granger] earned the ​respect of Members ​on both sides of the aisle through her steady leadership and deep belief in the importance of Congress fulfilling ​its constitutional responsibility ‌to invest in the American people," DeLauro said in ​a statement on Sunday.

title: U.S. exempts SpaceX's Starlink from FCC ban on foreign-made routers
description: Starlink has a Texas factory but also makes routers in Vietnam.
fullText:
The Trump administration today exempted SpaceX’s Starlink routers from the Federal Communications Commission ban on foreign-made routers.

A public notice issued by the FCC said Starlink routers received approval from the Department of War (also known as the Department of Defense). SpaceX’s exemption is good until February 1, 2028.

The FCC kicked off an industry-wide scramble when it updated the Covered List to include all consumer-grade routers made at least partly outside the US, except those that are granted exemptions. The Covered List includes devices deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to national security. Given that routers are generally built outside the US or at least contain foreign-made components, all major vendors need exemptions.

Netgear, Amazon, and other companies have previously been given exemptions. It’s widely expected that companies with Chinese ties will have the most trouble obtaining exemptions from the Trump administration, which alleges that foreign networking products pose national security risks and has pushed companies to make more devices in the US.

SpaceX has a factory in Texas, and some of its routers have the words “Made in the USA” printed on them, leading some to believe that it might be the only major router maker to escape the FCC’s wide-ranging ban. But other Starlink routers are made in Vietnam, as PCMag reported in April.

The FCC ban does not affect any routers that the FCC approved for sale before the rule change, but companies need the exemptions to get approval for future router models. Under the process announced by the FCC in March, router makers can ask the Department of War or Department of Homeland Security for a determination that their devices do not pose unacceptable risks to national security.

Netgear was the first major vendor to get an exemption, on April 14. Amazon then received an exemption for its Eero routers and the routers to be used for its Leo satellite service. TP-Link, which was founded in China but relocated its headquarters to the US, has not yet received an exemption. The full list of exemptions, formally known as “conditional approvals,” is available on the FCC website.

Drone makers also need exemptions under the same process because the FCC added drones to the Covered List last year. Chinese drone company DJI sued the FCC over the ban, and router makers could do the same if they are similarly unable to gain exemptions.

title: Trump shrugs off Cornyn’s hold on Blanche: ‘I heard he’s going through quite nicely’

President Trump brushed off concerns that Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) could hold up acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination in the Senate on Wednesday, saying he heard the process is going "quite nicely.

"I don't know what it is, but I haven't heard that there's a problem. I've heard he's going through quite nicely," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.

"All I can say is Todd Blanche is outstanding, and I thought it was pretty routine because he's good. You just wouldn't find a better person," he continued.

The president's comments come after Cornyn said his scheduled meeting with Blanche was canceled on Wednesday and that he was "not prepared to vote yes" on advancing Blanche's nomination.

"Maybe John Cornyn's upset with me because I didn't endorse him," Trump said, noting his decision earlier this year to back Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over Cornyn in the state's contested Republican Senate primary.

One Republican "no" vote on Blanche could stall his nomination in committee.

Cornyn has been pressuring the Justice Department on a controversial "anti-weaponization" fund.

The Texas senator told reporters Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) told him he needed to know by 4 p.m. whether Thursday morning's scheduled vote could proceed.

"So we still got a little time, and hopefully they now recognize the seriousness of this, and will be responding," Cornyn said.

Trump was also asked about Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) saying this week that he did not have the 50 votes necessary to advance a budget reconciliation bill through the Senate.

"Well, that's too bad for him. I mean, that's too bad for him and too bad for the Republican Party. He's got the votes. He should get it done. He should be able to get it done," Trump said.

Trump has also been pushing Thune and Senate Republicans to remove the filibuster to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, a law that would create new federal requirements for voter identification.

Thune insists there's not enough GOP support for such a move, and last week he suggested the White House help whip votes.

Asked if Thune was still "the man for the job," Trump told reporters, "Well, we're going to find out, and I'll let you know."

Talarico asserted that "police violence against communities of color, in particular our black community is nothing new, and has its roots in slavery and Jim Crow and mass incarceration."

He added that "this is just the latest iteration of the history of oppression this country has been a part of against African Americans."

He added that the discussion should be about "how do we take our criminal justice system at the state level, at the national level, and how do we make some fundamental changes to reflect our highest ideals and to really embody the country and state and the community that we want in the race to be."

"That's taking place," he continued, adding that communities are "figuring out how we reinvest our limited public funding into these community-based solutions that really start to address the underlying causes of our criminal justice system attempts to treat."

"That to me is really exciting," he said.

title: Delta-8, THC products come off Texas shelves Friday under new state ban
description: Starting Friday, Texas health officials are reclassifying Delta-8, Delta-10 and other THC isomers as controlled substances. Here's what to know.
fullText:
The deadline for various Delta-8 and THC products is here, as the products will be leaving shelves in Texas on Friday.

Starting July 31, the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) is set to reclassify Delta-8 THC and several other hemp-derived THC isomers — that are not delta-9 THC — as controlled substances in the state.

DSHS adopted new definitions for "Tetrahydrocannabinols" (THC) and "Marihuana Extract," with the change affecting products containing cannabinoids such as Delta-8, Delta-10, Delta-, and THCP, which was published in a July 10 public notice in the Texas Register.

In a July 27 social media post, the Texas Hemp Business Council said businesses cannot sell these products after July 31 and advised them to evaluate their inventory and prepare to remove or sell through products containing more than trace amounts of cannabinoids that fall within the reinstated definition.

Short answer: no under state and federal law.

However, Texas does allow medical use of low-THC cannabis through the state's Compassionate Use Program.

Products like delta-8 and THCA flower can create effects strikingly similar to those of delta-9 THC — the main intoxicating compound in cannabis, often called weed — which is illegal in Texas.

The key difference is how they're made and how they behave.

Delta-8 is a modified form of THC found in small amounts in hemp and usually converted from other cannabinoids. It can produce intoxicating or psychoactive effects, but it is not the same compound as Delta-9 THC.

THCA is sold as raw hemp flower and isn't intoxicating on its own.

But when it's heated — like by smoking or vaping — it turns into delta-9 THC, the same compound found in cannabis.

title: Talarico pulls ahead of Paxton by 5-points in new Texas Senate race poll
description: A new poll shows Democrat James Talarico leading Republican Ken Paxton by 5 points in the Texas Senate race. Here's a deeper look into what we know.
fullText:
A little over four months before Election Day, the Texas Senate race to replace U.S. Sen. John Cornyn remains contentious, as a new poll shows the Democratic candidate has opened a 5-point lead over the Republican candidate.

The Texas Public Opinion Research (TPOR) released a new poll on Tuesday, July 28, showing Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton trailing Democratic Texas state Rep. James Talarico.

The poll comes after two other polls in late June showed Paxton and Talarico tied within each poll's margin of error.

Here's a deeper look into the Texas Senate poll from TPOR.

The poll was conducted from July 15-17, polling 1,048 likely Texas voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. It was conducted by TPOR, which labels itself as a nonpartisan public opinion research group. Democratic strategist Luke Warford directs it.

The poll found that Talarico (45%) leads Paxton (40%) by 5 points in the U.S. Senate race — a 2-point increase from TPOR's post-runoff poll in May — with Talarico continuing to retain strong support from moderates and independents.

The poll also found that Talarico's performance is driven by voters saying Talarico better understands the economic challenges working Texans face than Paxton by 7 points, and that they trust Talarico to address affordability issues over Paxton by a 9-point margin.

However, the poll also found that 14% of Texas voters remain undecided, with 19% leaning toward Paxton, 10% toward Talarico, and 5% toward Libertarian Ted Brown.

Among Black and Latino voters, Talarico is strongly favored, leading Black voters by 63 points (71% to 8%) and Latino voters by 46 points (66% to 20%). Paxton, on the other hand, leads among white voters by 20 points (53% to 33%).

The poll was done days after The Texas Tribune and ProPublica published a joint investigation on July 7 alleging that Paxton had voted in six elections in the past two years using a former address. This led the Collin County Democratic Party to file a complaint on July 14 with the state's chief elections officer to determine whether Paxton had violated the state's election laws.

Paxton's campaign told USA TODAY on July 17 that it disputes the allegations made in the investigation and that Paxton is a "lawful, registered Texas voter in full compliance with the law."

Before this poll, two polls in June showed the race was deadlocked.

A New York Times/Siena poll, published on June 30, shows Paxton tied at 47% with Talarico.

The poll comes after a June 23 poll from the University of Texas and the Texas Politics Project that showed Paxton at 43% and Talarico at 42%, a 1-point gap within the survey's margin of error.

title: Falcons land WR help in 2027 NFL mock draft from CBS Sports
description: Falcons take 6-foot-3 Texas WR in 2027 NFL mock draft from CBS Sports
fullText:
There are some major question marks surrounding the Atlanta Falcons' roster as the team prepares to kick off training camp this week in Flowery Branch. From the starting quarterback competition to the battle for the No. 2 wide receiver job, Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski has much to figure out over the next month.

The team signed former first-round pick Jahan Dotson to replace speedster Darnell Mooney, but it's fair to question whether or not he's capable of filling that role. Dotson's career stats suggest otherwise, however, it's tough to produce when you're stuck behind two elite receivers, as he was in Philadelphia.

Former Georgia wide receiver Zachariah Branch appears to have a bright future, assuming his effectiveness isn't hindered by his lack of size. Depending on how this season goes, the Falcons may or may not be looking for a new No. 2 wide receiver in 2027.

Atlanta lands a perfect complement to Drake London in a new CBS Sports mock draft from Mike Renner. The Falcons were projected to take Texas wide receiver Cam Coleman with the sixth overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.

"Cam Coleman is a wildly explosive 6-foot-3, 200-pound wideout who spent the past two seasons stuck with poor quarterback play at Auburn," wrote Renner. "That changes this year as he heads to Texas to pair with Arch Manning. He should be a household name by season's end."

Coleman racked up 93 receptions for 1,306 receiving yards and 13 touchdowns (14.0 yards per catch) over the last two seasons at Auburn. The Falcons have dealt with similar quarterback issues over the past few years, so Coleman would feel right at home in Atlanta.

The Falcons did re-sign London to a four-year, $141 million contract extension during the offseason, however, there is still a clear lack of depth behind him. Branch could be a long-term option in the slot with No. 2 upside, but it wouldn't hurt to add to the receiver room in 2027.

For now, Atlanta is set to kick off training camp with its current wide receiver group. Although, we wouldn't be surprised to see the team add someone like Stefon Diggs or Keenan Allen before camp ends.

title: Nick Saban is a 'Mike Elko guy' and feels Texas A&M 'reloaded" in 2026
description: On the Pat McAfee Show, Nick Saban stated that Texas A&M has "reloaded" this offseason, and is on track to be a CFP contender in 2026.
fullText:
After making the College Football Playoff for the first time in program history, Texas A&M coach Mike Elko, entering his third season at the helm, saw a record 10 players selected in the 2026 NFL Draft and will return 65% of the 2025 roster, led by starting quarterback Marcel Reed, who threw for a career-high 3,169 yards, 25 touchdowns, and 12 interceptions.

On defense, losing unanimous All-American Edge Cashius Howell, who led the SEC with 11.5 sacks last season, stings, but was expected, and among A&M's 17 transfer portal additions this offseason, former Northwestern Edge Cashius Howell and several defensive line additions shore up the NFL departures, on paper, at least.

With Marcel Reed returning for his second full starting season, he'll be throwing to star junior receiver Mario Craver and Alabama transfer Isaiah Horton, who brings more size at 6'4", and should open up the middle of the field for Craver, Ashton Bethel-Roman, and Terry Bussey to thrive in short to intermediate throws.

This week, Mike Elko, alongside Marcel Reed, linebacker Daymion Sanford, and safety Marcus Ratcliffe, made the trip to Tampa (FL) for SEC Media Days to preview the 2026 season, and former Alabama coach Nick Saban, who has been a fan of Mike Elko since he was hired after the 2023 season, also attended the event as an analyst for ESPN/SEC Network, while making an appearance on the Pat McAfee Show, where he explained by he believes the Aggies have 'reloaded" to make another CFP run.

“Well, I’m a Mike Elko guy in terms of you know what he’s done at A&M,” Saban stated on The Pat McAfee Show. “They had 10 guys drafted. That’s more than they’ve ever had. They’ve got some of the highest rated recruiting classes, which they’ve never had in the past. Or when they did, they fell apart for whatever reasons, they’ve won more games. They play better defense. He’s one of the best defensive coaches in the country, scheme-wise, I think.

“And I think they’ve reloaded. I think they got some good players coming back. I think Marcel Reed is a really, really good quarterback who puts a lot of pressure on the defense. And I think they did a good job in a portal, and they did a good job of recruiting. I think they’re going to be one of the teams that people need to contend with in the SEC.”

Texas A&M's 2026 schedule is tough, facing road tests vs. LSU, Missouri, Alabama, South Carolina, and Oklahoma before hosting the Texas Longhorns at the end of the regular season, but given the defensive depth and Marcel Reed's experience under center, and after falling to Miami 10-3 in the first round of the CFP, Mike Elko bluntly stated “I show them our trophy case and it’s empty,” when asked about what keeps his team motivated heading into the new campaign.

title: Former Texas A&M DL cleared to return to Ravens after surgery
description: Former Aggie DL Nnamdi Madubuike, sidelined by a 2025 neck injury, has been cleared to return and begins 2026 on the Ravens’ PUP list.
fullText:
It has been a challenging year for former Texas A&M defensive lineman Nnamdi Madubuike, who went from one of the NFL’s premier interior disruptors to facing the possibility of never playing another down again.

After a breakout 2023 season and a new contract with the Baltimore Ravens, Madubuike followed up with a strong 2024 campaign, posting 6.5 sacks and 11 tackles for loss. Two games into the 2025 season, he already had two sacks and nine quarterback pressures, showing signs of returning to his dominant 2023 form until disaster struck. Following Baltimore’s Week 2 win over the Cleveland Browns, Madubuike began experiencing concerning symptoms in his neck and back.

The Ravens later confirmed a neck injury, sidelining him for the remainder of the season. Neck injuries are always unsettling, especially for defensive linemen, because the severity is often unclear and the risk of long‑term nerve damage increases dramatically in a sport built on violent contact.

Determined to get healthy and preserve his career, Madubuike underwent surgery in April. After months of rehab and consultations with specialists, an independent spine and cervical expert officially cleared him to return to football activities. With that encouraging news, the Ravens placed him on the PUP list entering the 2026 season.

The designation gives Madubuike the runway to ease back into the rhythm of an NFL offseason, rebuild strength, and gradually reintroduce contact under the supervision of Baltimore’s medical and performance staff. It’s a small but meaningful step toward seeing him back on the field at some point this season. A comeback that once felt far from guaranteed.

title: This red state is strengthening its grip as America's next economic heavyweight
description: IRS migration data reveal over $5 billion in wealth flowing into Texas as Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Austin fuel the state's population boom.
fullText:
The race to become America's next economic heavyweight may already have a frontrunner.

The latest Internal Revenue Service (IRS) migration data show billions of dollars in taxpayer wealth flowing into Texas, while Census figures show the state's largest metropolitan areas continue to outpace much of the country in population growth, strengthening a decades-long shift in America's economic center of gravity.

What's more, Texas isn't relying on a single boomtown. Dallas-Fort Worth added more residents than any metropolitan area in the country over the past year, while Houston, Austin and San Antonio also ranked among the nation's fastest-growing metros.

That unusual breadth gives Texas multiple engines of economic growth, providing businesses with larger labor pools, diversified industries and a broader customer base than states anchored by a single dominant city.

Billions In Taxpayer Income Are Leaving Two Iconic States — As A New Economic Map Emerges

The population boom has been accompanied by an influx of wealth. IRS migration data analyzed by the Tax Foundation show the Lone Star State gained more than $5 billion in adjusted gross income from interstate movers, while California and New York recorded multibillion-dollar losses.

"Capital follows where there is confidence," Texas Association of Business Chief Policy Officer Gabriela von zur Muehlen previously told Fox News Digital. "And right now there is a tremendous amount of confidence in Texas."

Von zur Muehlen said Texas' tax structure and predictable regulatory environment continue to attract businesses and investment from other states, helping reinforce the state's economic momentum.

While Florida attracted the nation's largest influx of taxpayer wealth and South Carolina posted the strongest inbound migration rate, Texas stood out by combining billions in new taxable income with rapid growth across Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Austin and San Antonio.

Economists say that combination matters because higher-income households bring spending, investment, entrepreneurship and tax revenue that can accelerate job creation, fuel commercial development and attract even more businesses. Over time, those forces can transform fast-growing metros into some of the nation's most influential economic hubs.

One Southern City You've Never Heard Of Is Growing Faster Than Anywhere Else In America

Unlike simple population counts, adjusted gross income offers a glimpse into the economic resources newcomers bring with them. Higher-income households can contribute disproportionately to consumer spending, investment and local tax collections, making income migration an important measure of a region's long-term economic strength.

title: Corey Seager takes live BP for first time since back injury again sidelined Rangers shortstop
description: Corey Seager took live batting practice Sunday for the first time since the Texas Rangers shortstop was sidelined by a back injury for the second time this season on July 1.  Seager finished the session with a home run and was planning to take live BP again Monday before what would appear to be a minor league rehab assignment.  The two-time World Series MVP played two games in the minors in early June when he was returning from a three-week absence because of lower back inflammation.
fullText:
ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Corey Seager took live batting practice Sunday for the first time since the Texas Rangers shortstop was sidelined by a back injury for the second time this season on July 1.

Seager finished the session with a home run and was planning to take live BP again Monday before what would appear to be a minor league rehab assignment.

The two-time World Series MVP played two games in the minors in early June when he was returning from a three-week absence because of lower back inflammation. Seager spent two more weeks on the injured list in June after getting a concussion.

“It's just tough to mimic some in-game stuff,” manager Skip Schumaker said of a possible rehab stint. “It's always up to the player. Because he missed so much time, we're going to discuss it. Looked like today was really good. See what it feels like tomorrow, and then we'll discuss the rehab assignment.”

Seager was removed from a game at Toronto in the first inning on June 30 because of back discomfort. The five-time All-Star is almost certain to play his fewest games since joining the Rangers in 2022.

Seager has been limited to 51 games in what has been the worst season of his career. He is hitting .182 with 10 home runs and 25 RBIs. Seager was in an 0-for-27 slide, the worst of his career, when he was sidelined by the back injury the first time.

After returning from the concussion, Seager played in three games before his back flared up. He wasn't ready to say he had a better handle on dealing with a balky back for a second time.

“I would love to tell you yes, but backs are not what you want,” Seager said.

The Rangers also are hopeful for the return soon of a pair of left-handers who haven't pitched in the big leagues since 2024.

Jordan Montgomery underwent the second elbow reconstruction surgery of his career last year when he was with Arizona. He joined the Diamondbacks after playing a key role for the Rangers when they won the World Series in 2023. Montgomery rejoined the Rangers on a one-year contract this year.

Cody Bradford, who had elbow surgery in June 2025, made 34 appearances in 21 starts over his first two big league seasons with the Rangers before getting shut down during spring training last year. Bradford also had a strong showing in the World Series when he was a rookie.

title: Talarico is trying to win back Hispanics along the Texas border who swung toward the GOP
description: The black campaign bus with “Talarico for Texas” across its side came to a steaming stop at Memo’s Restaurant along the U.S.-Mexico border.  “A lot of people, for some reason, especially the Hispanics...
fullText:
EAGLE PASS, Texas (AP) — The black campaign bus with "Talarico for Texas" across its side came to a steaming stop at Memo's Restaurant along the U.S.-Mexico border. Bibi Valdez's eyes lit up. She marched in heels over to the bus, phone camera trained on its door, chatting about the locals whose political leanings shifted two years ago.

"A lot of people, for some reason, especially the Hispanics, changed to Republican," she said as security guards created space for James Talarico, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate. "I just don't see what the logic was."

Talarico is on a quest to become the first Democrat to win a statewide election in Texas since 1994. Memo's Restaurant was one stop on a winding trip along the border this month, where he was searching for support from the predominantly Hispanic counties that became national political curiosities after the 2024 election.

Once consistently Democratic, most had voted for Republican President Donald Trump, some by a lot, as Hispanic voters shifted to the right nationally. Along this stretch of border, residents and elected leaders alike tend to point to two reasons: the rise in both border crossings and everyday prices. One dropped dramatically since 2024, and it wasn't the cost of eggs.

While Trump has tamped down on illegal border crossings — once Democrats' Achilles' heel — the cost of living is still high, giving Talarico a topic he's been hitting on repeat as he campaigns against Republican Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general.

Whether Talarico's message can sway Hispanic voters who moved to the GOP to return to the Democratic Party will help decide the Senate race, and could determine whether Democrats can win control of the Senate.

So Talarico, a former middle school teacher and state lawmaker, was taking time to shake hands and pose for photos with people outside Memo's Restaurant, which was at capacity with people wanting to see him. Valdez, waiting her turn, pondered aloud why those she knew had voted Republican.

"They thought a better economy, but obviously it didn't," she said, before beaming for a photo with the candidate.

Inside Memo's Restaurant, the crowd was revved up, shoulder to shoulder, below beating fans, as Talarico opened his speech.

"So many politicians show up at the border to demonize and weaponize," Talarico said. "We are doing the opposite. We are showing the beauty of our border communities."

It was one of the few times Talarico referenced the border during his stop, turning instead to an economy he says is rigged to help "mega donors" and criticizing Paxton as a "puppet politician" for the wealthy.

"We can't get ahead no matter how hard we work, no matter how much we save, because the system is rigged against us," he said.

Talarico is not the first Democratic Senate candidate in recent years to draw crowds and give the party hope of winning in the reliably Republican state. Beto O'Rourke went on a similar mission in 2018 and failed.

Republicans remain confident about Texas, but Democrats see some reason for optimism.

While Trump gained with Hispanic voters in 2024, opinions of the president have fallen among Hispanics overall since he took office, according to AP-NORC polling. Only 29% of Hispanic adults nationally approved of his performance as president in a June AP-NORC poll, an apparent drop from 41% at the start of his second term.

In communities along the Rio Grande, which defines the U.S.-Mexico border in Texas, the ebb and flow of migrants isn't an abstract political issue. People here still recall — often with empathy — hundreds huddled in reflective emergency blankets under a bridge, and the hit to local businesses and town coffers.

Little aid, many said, came from President Joe Biden's administration.

"It was a nightmare because of him. Now, you don't see no immigrants," said Hector Flores, 72, sitting with his two friends at a McDonald's in Maverick County, about an hour's drive south of Memo's Restaurant.

Maverick County had one of the sharpest swings toward Trump than any county in the country in 2024, from backing Biden by 10 percentage points in 2020 to supporting Trump by 19.

The three men of varying political persuasions weren't following the Senate race particularly closely. But the issues on their minds were the same ones Talarico and Paxton have been talking about, from high costs to ICE and social issues.

Under past presidents, costs were OK, said Eduardo "Lalo" Riojas, 73, who sat next to Flores. Now, "You go down to HEB to buy merchandise, groceries," he said, trailing off without the right English word.

"Yeah," said Riojas, who supports Talarico. "Mr. Trump is crazy."

For Flores, who works with orphanages across the border in Mexico, those high prices aren't making him question his Republican vote. Nor is he politically moved by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's sometimes lethal operations in the interior, which have ruffled some Trump supporters, both Hispanic and otherwise.

Mike Garcia, 76, who sat across from the two and said he voted for Trump three times in a row, was more wary.

"The ones they're killing, some of them, been here in the United States for years and years and got children," Garcia said.

He said Paxton, who has been impeached, then acquitted, and faced allegations of corruption and extramarital affairs, has a "horrible reputation." But he also is bothered by comments Talarico has made about God's gender, a statement Paxton has used to attack his opponent as he appeals to Texas voters' conservative values.

Garcia still didn't know which candidate he'll support come November.

Paxton has leaned more on immigration enforcement as an issue, including during his own border stop in the Rio Grande Valley.

Speaking in a circle of supporters in McAllen, Paxton first plugged the lawsuits he filed against the Biden administration over immigration enforcement, and his endorsement from the National Border Patrol Council.

He then returned to some of his core attacks on Talarico, including repeating the Democrat's statements that "God is nonbinary," which Talarico — a seminary student — said on the Texas House floor several years ago, citing Scripture.

His campaign's director of Hispanic outreach said Paxton has delivered what Hispanics want, including taking on criminals and companies that gouge consumers, and attacked Talarico as "wimpy."

"Hispanics know Ken Paxton is a strong man who shares our values, and we see in James Talarico a wimpy liberal," Alex Alarcon said. "No one looks at him and thinks, now there's a guy who'll protect us from the cartels."

Talarico didn't avoid talk about immigration enforcement completely during his border tour.

At a news conference, he stood in Sanderson, Texas, alongside local sheriffs to pledge investment in surveillance tech to catch illegal crossings and to hire more border patrol agents and immigration judges.

Later, after a town hall where voters aired their frustrations over affording rent, property taxes and healthcare, Talarico spoke with The Associated Press about what's been happening here.

"The Biden administration failed border communities like this, and so people were feeling disillusioned. They were open to an alternative and Republicans came down here with some big promises," he said.

Now, "they're seeing a lot of those promises weren't kept."

title: Tracking Corey Seager’s progress toward return to Texas Rangers
description: Texas Rangers star shortstop Corey Seager took live batting practice Friday, the latest step in his return to the active roster. ARLINGTON — All reports this week, from manager Skip...
fullText:
Texas Rangers star shortstop Corey Seager took live batting practice Friday, the latest step in his return to the active roster.

ARLINGTON — All reports this week, from manager Skip Schumaker to the man himself, indicated that Corey Seager is moving closer to returning to the Texas Rangers after a second absence caused by a bad back.

The shortstop on Friday attempted to simulate, as best he and the Rangers could, a rehab game at Globe Life Field. He took at-bats, then sat between them. He fielded groundballs and ran the bases, too.

The goal is for Seager to do that again Saturday or Sunday, depending on when the Rangers can find a reliable arm from Double A Frisco or Triple A Round Rock to come to Globe Life Field to pitch to the two-time World Series MVP.

A rehab assignment is being discussed. If left to Seager, he will go straight to the Rangers’ lineup once the medical staff gives him the green light. It might be left to Seager, though Schumaker won’t object if he wants to go somewhere for a few games.

The situation is fluid, it’s safe to say, but one thing that seems consistent is no one is willing to commit to a game when Seager will return. Maybe that’s the nature of back injuries, or maybe it’s the nature of Seager’s knack for being injured.

Maybe he’ll be back Monday for the finale in a critical series against the Mariners, which started Friday night. Maybe he’ll end up meeting the Rangers next Friday in Houston for another critical series against the Astros.

At least they’re talking about a return, and at the right time as the Rangers navigate the most important stretch of their season so far.

“I don’t feel strongly about him having an extended rehab. If he wanted a game or two, then I’m OK with that, too,” Schumaker said. “He just hasn’t played games in a while, but I would tell you the setup that we have going is almost like a rehab assignment. But it’s just tough to mimic certain things.”

Seager seems to have conquered the movements that made his back balk most — running and bending at the waist. That’s good, because a batter needs to run and a shortstop needs to bend at the waist.

The Rangers need Seager as they make their push for the playoffs, but, more urgently, their push to convince club brass to make additions at the Aug. 3 trade deadline. The Rangers entered Friday in first place in the American League West, albeit with a .500 record (51-51) and by only a half-game over the Mariners.

Friday’s game was the first of 10 remaining until the trade deadline, and a rough four games against the Mariners in this weekend wrap-around series might make the front office reconsider an investment in player acquisitions.

They might be completely sold with a good series.

While Seager appears close to returning, third baseman Josh Jung might need the injured list after a test of his left calf didn’t go well Friday. Schumaker said that Jung couldn’t get to full speed when running and might have been lucky to get to 50 percent.

Catcher Danny Jansen said that he’s not headed toward elbow surgery, at least not yet. He’s throwing at 90 feet with some oomph and will give things two more weeks before deciding if he can trudge through the rest of the season.

That’s curious timing, considering the Rangers just lost catcher Kyle Higashioka to a similar injury. That is now a need position for the Rangers at the deadline, though they might roll the dice if Jansen can manage the injury.

The Rangers also need bullpen help, though the healthy returns of starting pitchers Jack Leiter, Jordan Montgomery and Cody Bradford could produce multiple multi-inning relievers by mid-August. Montgomery, who was scheduled to make his final rehab start Friday night for Triple A Round Rock, could become a rotation option next week.

Leiter said that he plans to throw off a mound Saturday. If all goes well with his left ankle, he could begin what he hopes is a short buildup back to the rotation.

But the main injury news, as it is every time he is injured, is Seager. If he comes back, and if it’s soon, he could influence the Rangers’ decision-making ahead of the trade deadline.

Jeff Wilson, jwilson@alldlls.com
